runBy: Enbridge Gas + Save on Energy (IESO), with Ontario government support

Their advisors are NRCan-registered, but registration alone isn't enough — an assessment from any other company doesn't qualify.
headline: Up to $10,000 per home ($5,000 if heated with Enbridge gas), including $600 back on your two assessments, for insulation, windows, air sealing and more — if the follow-up assessment is done by December 31, 2026

amounts.label: Home energy assessments (paid after 2+ upgrades)
Insulation: attic $1,500 · walls $3,600 · foundation $2,300 · exposed floor $300
Windows & doors (at least 3 windows, or 1 door or skylight)
Air sealing (meet or beat the target)
Heat pump water heater
Bonus for 3 or more upgrades
Maximum per home if gas-heated (includes the $600)
Maximum per home if heated by electricity, oil, propane or wood (includes the $600)

whoQualifies: Ontario homeowners — not tenants — of detached, semi-detached, row or town homes, or mobile homes on a permanent foundation, who either heat mainly with Enbridge natural gas or are on Ontario's grid and heat with electricity, oil, propane or wood. Duplexes, triplexes, stacked townhouses, multi-unit buildings and homes occupied for less than 6 months don't qualify.
notes: The follow-up assessment must be booked by November 30, 2026 and completed by December 31, 2026, or within 180 days of the first assessment if that comes sooner, and rebates are paid only while program funding lasts. Starting now means booking the initial assessment within weeks and lining up contractors quickly. The $5,000 and $10,000 caps cover the whole assessment-path package, the $600 included, not just insulation. The program doesn't publish assessment prices: you pay the service organization up front and the $600 comes back at the end.
howToApply: Fill in the eligibility form on homerenovationsavings.ca. The program emails you its list of approved service organizations — you have to use one of these seven.
Book the initial assessment (about 2 hours) and pay the service organization. You get an EnerGuide rating and a report listing your recommended upgrades.
Hire contractors of your choice for at least two recommended upgrades. Nothing done before the initial assessment counts, and leave the ENERGY STAR labels on new windows and doors.
Book the follow-up assessment (about 1 hour) with the same service organization by November 30, 2026, for a visit no later than December 31, 2026 and within 180 days of the first.
Your advisor submits the file; you provide invoices and a property tax bill. Rebates arrive by e-Transfer within about 30 days, or by cheque within about 60.
gotchas: Only the seven approved service organizations can deliver this path. An EnerGuide assessment from any other company won't unlock these rebates.
The $600 assessment rebate is paid only after you finish two or more upgrades, and only once per home.
Gas-heated homes are capped at $5,000 in total, including the $600, so they can't reach the full $7,700 insulation amount.
Two windows earn nothing: the minimum is three windows, or one door, skylight or patio door.

Gas-heated homes qualify through Enbridge: the program is written for Enbridge Gas customers heating with natural gas, or for homes heated by electricity, oil, propane or wood. If your gas comes from Kitchener Utilities or Utilities Kingston, your home fits neither group, so confirm eligibility with the program before you plan around it.
An electrically heated home that switches to oil, propane or wood before the follow-up assessment loses eligibility.
You can't claim the same upgrade from another Enbridge, Save on Energy or Ontario program, and rebates can't exceed what you actually paid.
Enbridge and Save on Energy don't sell by phone or door to door. Treat unsolicited "program" calls as sales pitches.

Sarnia-area homes: the program's online form still mentions Enbridge's Sarnia Saves offer (up to $15,000) for N7S, N7T, N7V, N7W and N7X postal codes, Point Edward and Brights Grove, but Sarnia Saves has reached capacity and closed its intake, and Enbridge points those homeowners to Home Renovation Savings.

faq.q: Is the Home Renovation Savings assessment rebate still available?
faq.a: Yes, as of October 8, 2026, but only for homes that can finish in time. The follow-up assessment must be booked by November 30, 2026 and completed within 180 days of the first assessment or by December 31, 2026, whichever comes first, and rebates are paid only while program funding lasts.

faq.q: Can I use any energy advisor for the $600 rebate?
faq.a: No. You have to book through one of seven approved service organizations: AmeriSpec, Canada Energy Audit, Greenbrain, Energuy, Energy Werx, NRGwise or The Home Inspectors Group. Their advisors are NRCan-registered, but being registered on its own isn't enough.

faq.q: Do community non-profits like Windfall or Reep qualify?
faq.a: Not for this program. Windfall Ecology Centre, Reep Green Solutions and other NRCan-licensed organizations deliver official EnerGuide evaluations, often at published prices, but they aren't among the seven approved organizations, so their assessments don't qualify for the $600 rebate or the assessment-path upgrade rebates.

faq.q: How much can I get in total?
faq.a: Up to $5,000 per home if you heat with Enbridge natural gas, or up to $10,000 if you heat with electricity, oil, propane or wood — both including the $600 assessment rebate. Finishing three or more upgrades also earns a $500 bonus.

faq.q: When is the $600 assessment rebate paid?
faq.a: After the follow-up assessment, once at least two recommended upgrades are done. You pay for both assessments up front.

faq.q: Can tenants apply?
faq.a: No. Only the owner can participate, though an owner can apply for each eligible home they own.

whoQualifies: Ontario homeowners. Heat pump amounts depend on how you heat today; gas-heated homes qualify at lower amounts and can keep the furnace as backup. Replacing an existing heat pump doesn't qualify, homes occupied for less than 6 months are excluded, and solar has to power the home itself (no net metering).
notes: Even without a required assessment, audit-first usually changes what you buy: a proper heat-loss calculation right-sizes the heat pump, and insulating first can shrink it. The program's attic and smart thermostat pages no longer list the installation and submission deadlines (November 30 and December 31, 2026) that we showed earlier, and the heat pump page lists no end date. The smart thermostat rebate is $125 on its current page, as an instant code (The Home Depot in-store; Best Buy, Copeland Sensi, ecobee or Mysa online) or by uploading your receipt within 60 days; the program's help page still says $100.
howToApply: Fill in the eligibility form for the upgrade you want on homerenovationsavings.ca.

Heat pumps: choose a participating HVAC contractor, who submits the pre-installation application. Solar and batteries: any licensed electrical contractor can apply for you. Wait for written approval before buying anything.
Have the work installed. The contractor files the completion paperwork within 30 days.
Heat pump rebates arrive by cheque within about 60 days of approval.
Smart thermostats and appliances are simpler: buy, then upload your receipt within 60 days — or get a thermostat discount code before you buy.
gotchas: The $12,000 headline is for ground-source systems. A cold-climate air-source heat pump tops out at $7,500, or $2,000 if you heat with Enbridge gas.
Anything installed before written pre-approval gets no heat pump or solar rebate.
A battery on its own doesn't qualify, and solar systems can't be net-metered.

Oil-heated homes must size the new electric heating (heat pump plus any electric backup) to replace the oil heat completely, and have a TSSA-registered contractor deal with the oil tank. Homes heated by electricity or wood need a heat pump sized mainly for heating (NRCan sizing option C or D); gas-heated homes can keep the furnace as backup.

Attic rebates are 50% of the after-tax cost, up to the tier maximum ($1,250 only if your attic is R-12 or less today), and have to go through one of the program's participating contractors. Registration for new attic contractors is closed, so confirm one serves your area before you plan around it. The work must cover 100% of the roof assembly.

Gas-heated homes qualify through Enbridge: the program is written for Enbridge Gas customers heating with natural gas, or for homes heated by electricity, oil, propane or wood. If your gas comes from Kitchener Utilities or Utilities Kingston, your home fits neither group, so confirm eligibility with the program before you plan around it.
You can't claim the same upgrade from another Enbridge, Save on Energy or Ontario program, and total funding can't exceed your cost.
Replacing an existing heat pump doesn't qualify; the rebates are for first-time installations, and new homes must have been occupied for at least 6 months.

faq.q: Does a gas-heated home get a heat pump rebate?
faq.a: Yes: up to $2,000 for an air-source heat pump or $3,000 for ground-source, and you can keep the furnace as backup.

faq.q: Is the Ontario heat pump rebate really $12,000?
faq.a: Only for ground-source (geothermal) systems in homes heated by electricity, oil, propane or wood. Cold-climate air-source heat pumps get $1,250 per ton, up to $7,500.

faq.q: Do I need an energy audit for these rebates?
faq.a: No, but heat pumps and solar need written pre-approval before installation — and an audit's heat-loss calculation is still the best way to size a heat pump.

faq.q: Is there a rebate for a home battery on its own?
faq.a: No. Storage only qualifies when it's installed with new rooftop solar, and the system can't be net-metered.

faq.q: How much is the attic insulation rebate?
faq.a: It depends on what's there now, and you have to reach R-50: up to $1,250 if the attic is R-12 or less, $1,000 from above R-12 to R-25, and $800 from above R-25 to R-35. Cathedral ceilings and flat roofs get $650–$750. The rebate is 50% of your after-tax cost, up to those amounts, and the work has to be done by a participating contractor. The attic page doesn't currently list an installation deadline.

faq.q: Do rented heat pumps qualify?
faq.a: Yes, whatever fuel you heat with: $500 per ton up to $2,000 for a cold-climate air-source heat pump, or $3,000 for a ground-source system. Pre-approval is still required before installation.

faq.q: How much is the smart thermostat rebate?
faq.a: $125, one per household, on the program's smart thermostat page (its help page still says $100). Get an instant code before you buy (The Home Depot in-store, or Best Buy, Copeland Sensi, ecobee or Mysa online), or buy anywhere and upload your receipt within 60 days.

faq.q: When do the Home Renovation Savings heat pump rebates end?
faq.a: The heat pump page lists no installation deadline, submission deadline or end date (checked October 8, 2026). The assessment path is different: its follow-up assessment must be done by December 31, 2026.

name: Toronto Home Energy Loan Program (HELP)
auditRequirementNote: An EnerGuide assessment before and after the work, by an NRCan-registered energy advisor, is required for most projects. Heat-pump-only and rooftop-solar-only projects are exempt — the installer signs an attestation instead.

whoQualifies: Owners of detached, semi-detached and row houses, duplexes, triplexes and low-rise buildings (up to 3 storeys and 6 units) in Toronto. Every owner on title must agree, your mortgage lender has to consent in writing, and you can't have repeated overdue tax or utility accounts. 20-year terms are only for projects that include solar, geothermal, windows or heat pumps.
notes: HELP is financing, not a rebate, and the City says it can be combined with provincial, federal and utility rebates. A common Toronto path is HELP to pay for the work, then Home Renovation Savings rebates on top. The City sets HELP's fixed rates every quarter. The table on its page was valid until September 30, 2026 (3.34% for 5 years, 4.01% for 10, 4.46% for 15 and 4.75% for 20), and it was still the posted table when we checked on October 8, 2026 (page last modified September 28), so check the City's current rate table before you apply.
howToApply: Apply online with the City. Expect a reply in about 5–7 business days; if you have a mortgage, the City sends a lender-consent form.
Once the City has your lender's consent, it sends a funding offer (about 5–7 business days).
Book the "before" EnerGuide assessment, get contractor quotes, and submit your funding request. Heat-pump-only and solar-only projects just need quotes.
Sign the Property Owner Agreement the City drafts (up to 15 business days). You can then ask for up to 30% of the loan in advance.

Do the work and the "after" assessment, then send the completion report, invoices and your new EnerGuide label. Final payment follows in about 10 business days, and repayment on your tax bill starts 60 days after the file closes.
gotchas: The 10%-of-assessed-value cap often bites first: a home assessed at $900,000 can borrow at most $90,000, and that includes the interest and the 2% fee.
You pay contractors and receive most of the money after the work is verified, so plan cash flow for about 70% of the project.
The loan stays with the house. If you sell, pay it off or the buyer takes over the balance — disclose it.
Your mortgage lender has to consent in writing, so start that paperwork early.
The City's separate HELP rebates were fully subscribed and closed in January 2025; only the loans remain.

faq.q: Do I need an energy audit for a Toronto HELP loan?
faq.a: Yes, before and after the work, unless the project is only a heat pump or only rooftop solar.

faq.q: What are the Toronto HELP interest rates?
faq.a: Rates are fixed for the loan's term, but the City resets them every quarter. The last posted table, valid until September 30, 2026 and still on the City's page on October 8, 2026, was 3.34% for 5 years, 4.01% for 10, 4.46% for 15 and 4.75% for 20, plus a 2% administrative charge. Check the City's current rate table before you apply.

faq.q: What happens to a HELP loan if I sell my house?
faq.a: It stays with the property as a charge on the tax bill. You can pay it off at any time, or the buyer takes over the remaining balance.

faq.q: Is the money paid up front?
faq.a: Up to 30% can be advanced once your agreement is signed; the rest is paid after the work is completed and verified.

faq.q: Can condo owners apply?
faq.a: Condos aren't among the eligible property types. The program covers houses, duplexes, triplexes and small low-rise buildings.

name: CMHC Eco Improvement premium refund
seoTitle: CMHC Eco Improvement (2026): the 25% energy-efficiency rebate on your mortgage insurance premium
seoDescription: CMHC Eco Improvement is an energy-efficiency rebate for recent buyers: a 25% refund of your CMHC mortgage insurance premium after $20,000 of energy upgrades, claimed within 2 years of closing. Who qualifies, what counts and how to apply, verified October 8, 2026.
auditRequirementNote: No EnerGuide evaluation is required — the test is money spent on eligible work. Include an EnerGuide report or label if you have one.
headline: A 25% energy-efficiency rebate on your CMHC mortgage insurance premium after $20,000 of energy renovations

amounts.label: Refund of your CMHC mortgage insurance premium
Minimum eligible work after purchase
Time to apply, counted from your mortgage closing

whoQualifies: Buyers of existing homes, including eligible condominium units and prefabricated homes, with a CMHC-insured mortgage who complete at least $20,000 of eligible energy-efficient work after purchase: insulation, windows, doors, roofing or air sealing; heating, ventilation, air conditioning or heat pumps; or solar, wind or geothermal. Covers owner-occupied loans (1–4 units) and small rental loans (2–4 units).
notes: Often missed by recent buyers: the 2-year clock starts at your mortgage closing, not when the work is done, and the improvements themselves can be done up to 2 years after closing. Mortgages insured by Sagen or Canada Guaranty don't qualify: their 25% energy-efficiency refunds only cover newly built homes.
howToApply: Close on your home with a CMHC-insured mortgage — your lender or broker can confirm which insurer you have.
Complete at least $20,000 of eligible energy renovations after you buy.
Fill in CMHC's Eco Improvement form. Every borrower signs it, and it needs your CMHC loan number.
Send it with all paid invoices and a void cheque (plus any EnerGuide report or label) by email, fax or mail within 24 months of closing.
CMHC says processing currently takes about 8–10 weeks. The refund arrives by direct deposit.
gotchas: The deadline is 24 months from your mortgage closing, not from the end of the renovation.
Only CMHC-insured mortgages qualify. Sagen and Canada Guaranty refunds cover new builds only, with no renovation equivalent.
Keep every paid invoice — the $20,000 test is proven with receipts.

faq.q: Is CMHC Eco Improvement an energy-efficiency rebate?
faq.a: In effect, yes: CMHC calls it a partial premium refund. If you bought with a CMHC-insured mortgage and complete at least $20,000 of qualifying energy-efficient renovations, CMHC refunds 25% of your mortgage insurance premium by direct deposit. Verified October 8, 2026.

faq.q: Do I need an EnerGuide evaluation for CMHC Eco Improvement?
faq.a: No. The test is $20,000 of eligible work after purchase; submit an EnerGuide report or label if you have one.

faq.q: What's the deadline for CMHC Eco Improvement?
faq.a: Apply within 2 years of your mortgage closing date; the improvements can be completed up to 2 years after closing. CMHC says processing currently takes about 8 to 10 weeks.

faq.q: How much will I get back?
faq.a: 25% of the CMHC mortgage insurance premium you paid, by direct deposit.

faq.q: My mortgage is insured by Sagen or Canada Guaranty — is there an equivalent?
faq.a: Not for renovations. Both insurers' energy-efficiency refunds apply to newly built homes only.

faq.q: Do condos qualify?
faq.a: Yes. CMHC says eligible condominium units and prefabricated homes are included, as long as the mortgage is CMHC-insured and the $20,000 of qualifying work is done after purchase.

name: Canada Greener Homes Affordability Program
runBy: Natural Resources Canada (moving to Environment and Climate Change Canada), delivered by provincial partners
auditRequirementNote: No EnerGuide evaluation is needed to apply. Where an assessment or home visit is part of the program, the provincial partner arranges it.
headline: Free retrofits for low-to-median-income households through provincial partners in BC, Manitoba, Nova Scotia, PEI and Quebec (Quebec's 2026–27 intake has closed) — not available in Ontario

amounts.label: Insulation, air sealing and heat pumps, installed for qualifying households

whoQualifies: Low-to-median-income homeowners and, in some provinces, tenants. Each provincial partner sets its own income limits and home types. NRCan's page (updated August 31, 2026) lists BC (BC Hydro, FortisBC), Manitoba (Efficiency Manitoba), Nova Scotia (HomeWarming and the African Nova Scotian Communities Retrofit program), PEI and Quebec (Hydro-Québec, whose 2026–27 registration has ended). Newfoundland and Labrador's takeCHARGE has launched an income-eligible TakeCharge Greener Homes Program "delivered in partnership with the Government of Canada" for projects completed after October 5, 2026, but NRCan doesn't list it yet. Ontario, New Brunswick, Alberta, Saskatchewan and the territories have no listed partner.
notes: The program is moving from NRCan to Environment and Climate Change Canada; questions go to enviroinfo@ec.gc.ca. We'll update this page when NRCan lists another province.
howToApply: Find your province's delivery partner on NRCan's program page — you apply to them, not to Ottawa.

Check their income limits. BC Hydro's run from $51,100 for one person to $135,100 for seven or more; Efficiency Manitoba's from $46,264 to $122,432; PEI's insulation program requires household income under $55,000.
Apply with proof of income for the adults in your household, plus landlord consent if you rent where tenants are eligible.
The partner arranges the assessment or home visit, then its contractors install the upgrades at no cost to you.
gotchas: Rules differ a lot by province: who qualifies, which home types, and whether renters can apply.
Hydro-Québec's registration for the 2026–27 season has ended; it is processing the applications already received.
This isn't the old Greener Homes Grant coming back: it's income-tested and only runs through provincial partners.
Ontario households can't apply.
Be wary of door-to-door or phone offers claiming to be the program; NRCan says it hasn't approved any third party to contact homeowners about it.

faq.q: Is the Greener Homes Affordability Program available in Ontario?
faq.a: Not as of October 8, 2026. Ontario has no delivery partner; NRCan lists BC, Manitoba, Nova Scotia, PEI and Quebec.

faq.q: Can renters qualify?
faq.a: In BC, Manitoba and Quebec, yes — landlord consent may be needed. PEI's program is for owner-occupied homes.

faq.q: How do I apply?
faq.a: Through your provincial partner, not NRCan. The partner checks your income and arranges the work.

faq.q: Do I need an EnerGuide evaluation first?
faq.a: No. Where an assessment is part of the program, the partner arranges it for you.

faq.q: Is Newfoundland and Labrador part of the Affordability Program?
faq.a: Not on NRCan's list yet. takeCHARGE launched an income-eligible TakeCharge Greener Homes Program, "delivered in partnership with the Government of Canada", that covers up to 100% of approved upgrades completed after October 5, 2026, including a limited number of no-cost heat pumps.

faq.q: I finished my retrofit but never got paid. What can I do?

faq.q: Does LogisVert require an energy audit?

faq.q: Can I still get LogisVert money for insulation?

auditRequirementNote: The program has ended; no application path exists. Audits in Saskatchewan are now purely diagnostic — and in this climate, still routinely worth the fee.
headline: Ended April 2026 — what's left is the Home Renovation Tax Credit, SaskEnergy equipment rebates and free upgrades for income-qualified homes

Saskatchewan Home Renovation Tax Credit: 10.5% of expenses above $1,000, up to $5,000 ($6,000 for seniors)

whoQualifies: No one, for the rebate. For the tax credit: owners renovating their principal residence in Saskatchewan, for expenses incurred on or after October 1, 2024, claimed on a 2025 or later tax return.
notes: Our earlier link for this program (saskatchewan.ca) now returns "page not found"; SaskPower and SaskEnergy both confirm the rebate ended in April 2026, without giving a day. SaskEnergy's remaining residential rebates are for high-efficiency gas furnaces ($325), boilers ($750–$800) and tankless or condensing water heaters ($1,000), for replacements only, within 120 days of installation. Income-qualified households can get free upgrades through SaskPower's Energy Assistance Program, and participants may qualify for a free high-efficiency furnace through SaskEnergy's Heating Affordability Program. In Saskatoon, the City's Home Energy Loan Program lends $1,000–$40,000 (up to $60,000 with a 50% energy cut) at 2026 rates of 3.24%–4.83%, plus a $1,000 rebate toward energy audits for loan participants.
howToApply: There's nothing to apply for: the rebate ended in April 2026.
Keep receipts for renovation work on your home. The Home Renovation Tax Credit is claimed on your personal income tax return.
Replacing a gas furnace, boiler or water heater? Check SaskEnergy's Residential Equipment Replacement Rebate and apply within 120 days of installation.
Income-qualified? Apply for SaskPower's free Energy Assistance Program; participants may then qualify for SaskEnergy's free furnace upgrade.
In Saskatoon, look at the City's Home Energy Loan Program, which finances insulation, windows and heat pumps.
gotchas: Any site or salesperson promising this rebate today is out of date; treat it as a screening test.
The tax credit is non-refundable: it reduces the provincial income tax you owe, and it tops out at $420 a year ($525 for seniors).
SaskEnergy's rebates are for replacement gas equipment, not heat pumps.
Your own labour, routine maintenance, appliances and financing costs don't count toward the tax credit.

faq.q: Is the Saskatchewan Home Efficiency Retrofit Rebate still available?
faq.a: No. SaskPower and SaskEnergy say it ended in April 2026, and neither lists a replacement rebate on its program pages (checked October 8, 2026).

faq.q: Is there a Saskatchewan government window grant?
faq.a: There's no window grant, but windows and doors are eligible expenses for the Saskatchewan Home Renovation Tax Credit: 10.5% of expenses above $1,000, up to $5,000, so at most $420 a year ($525 for seniors). It's non-refundable and claimed on your income tax return.

faq.q: Is there a heat pump rebate in Saskatchewan?
faq.a: Not from SaskPower or SaskEnergy as of October 8, 2026: neither lists a residential heat pump rebate. Saskatoon's Home Energy Loan Program finances cold-climate air-source and ground-source heat pumps.

faq.q: Why list a dead program at all?
faq.a: Because stale advertising outlives programs, and knowing a promise is dead is worth as much as knowing a program is live. A contractor citing this rebate in 2026 has told you how current the rest of their pitch is.

headline: Yukon pays up to $10,500 toward a heat pump (up to $24,000 if income-qualified) and up to $12,000 for wall insulation; the NWT's Arctic Energy Alliance subsidizes EnerGuide evaluations and insulation; Nunavut support runs through the Housing Corporation

whoQualifies: Territorial homeowners, per each program's rules. Yukon's heat pump rebates need a home at least six months old, an eligible cold-climate or ground-source unit, and the existing heating kept as backup; the Affordable Heat Pump Program adds income limits (after-tax income under $53,820 for one resident, up to $184,000 for five or more) and pre-approval. NWT rebates follow the Arctic Energy Alliance's program year (April 1, 2026 to March 31, 2027).
notes: The territories run delivery organizations rather than big rebate portals. Yukon's Energy Branch pays the largest northern heat pump rebates (oil-heated applicants to the Affordable Heat Pump Program also get $250 from NRCan), plus insulation, air sealing and window rebates; an energy assessment is required before the insulation and air sealing rebate. The NWT's Arctic Energy Alliance no longer gives rebates for heating systems that use fossil fuels and lists no heat pump rebate; it subsidizes EnerGuide evaluations ($200 + GST for a house) and pays for insulation, programmable thermostats (50% up to $150) and wood or pellet stoves. Homes in Nunavut were never eligible for the federal oil-to-heat-pump program because of grid requirements.
howToApply: Yukon: start at the Energy Branch's rebate pages; heat pump rebates are paid within 12 weeks, and the Affordable Heat Pump Program needs pre-approval before you install.
Yukon insulation and air sealing: complete the required energy assessment before applying, and keep receipts dated within a year of your application.
NWT: contact the Arctic Energy Alliance for a subsidized EnerGuide evaluation and its rebate forms.
Nunavut: the Nunavut Housing Corporation's homeownership programs offer advice on repairs, renovations, financing and energy conservation; start with its current program list.
Everywhere: northern fuel prices make a measured baseline worth more, not less.
gotchas: Yukon heat pump rebates require keeping your existing heating as backup; electric backup must be enrolled in Yukon Energy's Peak Smart Home program.
NWT rebates no longer cover heating systems that burn fossil fuels.
Southern contractor assumptions (and southern heat pump specs) don't transfer to northern design temperatures; get local advice on equipment.
The federal oil-to-heat-pump program never applied in Nunavut and is now closed everywhere; ignore any pitch built on it.

faq.q: What energy programs exist in Canada's territories?
faq.a: Yukon's Energy Branch rebates (heat pumps up to $10,500, or $24,000 income-qualified; insulation, air sealing and windows), the NWT's Arctic Energy Alliance (subsidized EnerGuide evaluations, insulation, thermostats and wood stoves), and the Nunavut Housing Corporation's homeownership programs. Verified October 8, 2026.

faq.q: Is there a heat pump rebate in the territories?
faq.a: In Yukon, yes: 50% of costs up to $10,500 for an existing home, or 100% up to $24,000 through the income-qualified Affordable Heat Pump Program. The NWT's Arctic Energy Alliance lists no heat pump rebate, and we found none for Nunavut.

faq.q: Why do audits matter more in the North?
faq.a: Because heating fuel is expensive and the winters are long, every air leak and thin assembly the audit finds costs more than it would down south, and envelope failures at northern temperatures can be safety issues, not just comfort issues.
